issues.item: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: This trigger is hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the profile. For a 21-year-old married male relief worker in a war zone, military topics and Arabic shouting fit the reported trauma context, but 'my ex' is relationship-specific and not plausibly linked to the war-zone trauma as presented. It also does not connect well to the accompanying threat and memory items, which are clearly organized around combat/civilian danger cues rather than intimate-relationship themes.

vignette:
Aleksander Nowak is a 21-year-old Polish-American man who works for a faith-based social ministry organisation and who, until several months ago, had considered his work the most meaningful thing in his life. He is married, newly so, and his wife had supported his decision to deploy as a relief worker to an active conflict zone in the Middle East, believing as he did that the work was urgent and necessary. What happened there has made it difficult for him to believe in urgency, necessity, or much else.

Aleksander had been stationed at a distribution point near a contested urban corridor. The work was logistically complex and emotionally demanding, but he had felt capable. Then, during what began as a routine supply handoff, a firefight erupted in the street adjacent to the compound. He was on the ground when the shooting started, surrounded by colleagues and civilians. People around him were screaming - in Arabic, in English, in languages he could not identify - and he had pressed himself against a concrete wall for what felt like hours but was, he was later told, approximately eleven minutes. A man he had been working alongside was struck and fell within his line of sight. Aleksander could not reach him. He remained pinned, certain he was about to die, listening to the shouting grow closer and then recede. When it was over, he was physically unharmed. He was evacuated within forty-eight hours and returned to the United States two weeks later.

The months since have been disorienting in a way he struggles to articulate. The memory of those eleven minutes does not feel like something that ended. When he tries to describe it to his wife - which he has done only twice, haltingly - the terror returns as fully as it was present in that corridor, and he has stopped trying. He had once assumed that surviving something meant, eventually, being on the other side of it. He has come to feel that no such other side exists for him. The memory carries a quality that unsettles him perhaps more than anything else: it is so extreme, so unlike anything in his prior twenty-one years of life, that he sometimes cannot fully accept it as his own history. It feels simultaneously unreal and inescapable.

His days are shaped by a vigilance that follows him into ordinary spaces. At his ministry office, where he now works primarily with resettlement cases, he finds himself scanning the room when colleagues raise their voices. A co-worker who gestured sharply during a meeting last month sent Aleksander's body into an immediate state of alarm that took the rest of the afternoon to subside. When clients who are Arabic-speaking become animated or distressed and raise their voices, he has begun excusing himself from those meetings, telling his supervisor he needs a moment, though he has not explained why. His work with refugee families - people who have fled the same kinds of violence he briefly witnessed - has become both more fraught and more isolating. He feels he cannot tell them what he carries, and he cannot pretend he does not carry it.

At home, he stays up well past midnight most nights, finding the transition to sleep intolerable. When he does sleep, he wakes in the dark and lies still, listening, checking. His wife has noticed and has asked. He has deflected. He has also begun declining the small pleasures she proposes - a dinner with friends, a film she thought he would enjoy - not because he is indifferent to her but because he has come to feel that allowing himself to feel hopeful or happy would be a kind of lie, or perhaps a vulnerability he cannot afford. He spends a portion of most evenings turning over the sequence of events from that day, tracing the decisions and contingencies, wondering what might have changed the outcome for the man who fell.

What finally brought him to seek help was a conversation at work in which a colleague casually mentioned a news story about military operations in the region. Aleksander left the room, sat in a bathroom stall for twenty minutes, and then called the ministry's employee assistance line. He is most afraid, he said at intake, that this is simply who he is now. What he is hoping, though he said it quietly, is that it isn't.
